performers: Marian Anderson, contralto; San Francisco Symphony Orchestra; Pierre Monteux, conductor
intro: Marian Anderson sings “Nun will die Sonn’ so hell aufgeh’n”, the first of the Kindertotenlieder, with Pierre Monteux and the San Francisco Symphony in 1950. The song opens with oboe and horn and ends with small bells, and Rückert’s text sets a father’s loss against the rising morning sun.

sections.label: A · Oboe and horn
sections.mNote: The contralto enters over two wind lines.

sections.label: A′ · Voice with flute and bassoon
sections.mNote: Flute doubles the voice; bassoon repeats rising steps.

sections.label: B · Violins
sections.mNote: Horn and voice alternate the opening phrases.

sections.label: A″ · The little lamp
sections.mNote: Oboe, flute and glockenspiel accompany the last couplet.

cues.title: Opening, oboe, horn and contralto
cues.text: A horn moves slowly beneath the oboe’s short steps. Anderson enters with the line “Nun will die Sonn’ so hell aufgeh’n” (now the sun will rise so brightly). On the first page there is little scoring besides the contralto and these two wind instruments.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460, p. 3; Rückert’s opening line, our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Deaths of Rückert’s children
cues.text: Friedrich Rückert’s children Luise and Ernst died on 31 December 1833 and 16 January 1834. In his grief he wrote more than four hundred poems, none meant for print. Mahler later chose five of them.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik, Universal Edition introduction to Kindertotenlieder (autumn 2008), gives the two dates and the 400-odd poems, published after Rückert’s death: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Kindertotenlieder/P0045027. The Mahler Foundation counts 428 poems and says they were not intended for publication: https://mahlerfoundation.org/mahler/compositions/kindertotenlieder/kindertotenlieder-introduction/

cues.title: Second couplet, return of the opening
cues.text: The second couplet sets the father’s “mir allein” (me alone) against a sun that shines on everyone. Mahler brings back the opening with a flute doubling Anderson’s line and the bassoon below. The vocal rhythm is changed so that the stress falls on the bereaved person.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 6–8; Rückert’s second couplet, our translation. Woltjer explains the changed vocal rhythm and flute doubling: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Third couplet, horn melody
cues.text: The horn plays the melody the voice sang earlier. Anderson sings a new line against it, and the oboe rises. At “ew’ge Licht” (eternal light) the phrase passes to the violins and continues after the sung words end.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 9–14, third couplet; our translation. Woltjer discusses the horn’s vocal theme and the instrumental continuation: https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Footnote in the full score, 1905
cues.text: In a footnote on the first page of the score, Mahler asked that the five songs be treated as one inseparable whole. He added that their continuity was to be kept even against the applause that would normally follow a “number”.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, C. F. Kahnt full score, plate 4460 (1905), printed p. 3, footnote: “Diese 5 Gesänge sind als ein einheitliches, untrennbares Ganzes gedacht …”; our translation. https://urresearch.rochester.edu/fileDownloadForInstitutionalItem.action?itemId=18417&itemFileId=62425 The same instruction is printed on the title page of the 1905 vocal score: https://www.mahlercat.org.uk/Pages/KtL/KtLprints.htm

cues.title: Final couplet, return of opening melody
cues.text: The last couplet sets the line “Ein Lämplein verlosch in meinem Zelt” (a little lamp went out in my tent). The opening melody returns, with oboe and flute playing close around the contralto.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 14–17; Rückert’s final couplet, our translation. The section boundary marks the returning passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Closing bars, harp and glockenspiel
cues.text: Anderson’s last phrase salutes the world’s joyful light. Harp and glockenspiel continue after the voice stops. The score ends with a full bar of rests under fermatas.
cues.evidence: Kahnt full score, p. 17: final words, harp and glockenspiel, then a bar of rests with fermatas. The existing late cue lies within this closing passage.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The oboe returns over the harp
transitions.to: A′ · Voice with flute and bassoon
transitions.how: The oboe begins its opening phrase again while the harp alternates between D-minor notes. The glockenspiel continues its single strokes above. The shortened introduction leads to a changed vocal rhythm, with the flute doubling Anderson and the bassoon repeating C♯–D below.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 6–8; Woltjer, song I, bars 22 onwards. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html

transitions.title: Horn and contralto exchange phrases
transitions.from: A′ · Voice with flute and bassoon
transitions.how: The horn extends the closing phrase of the second couplet over low clarinet and bassoon. Rising oboe figures lead into the next passage. The horn then plays the earlier vocal tune, the contralto sings alternate phrases with it, and the harmony moves between D minor and D major.
transitions.evidence: Kahnt full score, pp. 9–13; Woltjer, song I, bars 36–59. https://geertwoltjer.nl/Songs/MahlerAnalysis/Mahler1.html

transitions.title: Return of the oboe’s first phrase
transitions.how: The flute plays its running notes more softly around the returning oboe melody. The horns hold notes below, and the glockenspiel plays between the phrases. Mahler marks the passage zurückkehrend (returning), and the D-minor tune returns for the last couplet.

source.title: Mahler, Kindertotenlieder, full score (C. F. Kahnt, plate 4460)
source.locator: Song I, printed pp. 3–17: oboe and horn introduction, muted strings, the violins’ rising phrases and the final harp and glockenspiel.

timeline.note: Opening duet: oboe above the first horn, without voice or strings.
Harp and muted violas and cellos accompany Anderson’s first stanza.
The oboe’s opening phrase returns as the father sings of his own loss.
The first violins enter with a high melody as the voice reaches the words about eternal light.
Flute and oboe bring back the opening phrases before the last stanza.
Harp and strings accompany the father’s blessing of the world’s joyful light.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
